author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Mayadevi Temple and Village Mound, Lumbini (Rummindei), Rupandehi, Nepal
evidence: Ch. 3 (Coningham, Acharya, Tremblay) on the JFIT-UNESCO excavations of 2011–13: the Village Mound (police parade ground trench, 4.5 m deep) has habitation from c. 1300 BCE to the 6th c. CE; under the Mayadevi Temple a straight line of post holes of the mid-6th c. BCE (radiocarbon and OSL) defined an open central space where soil micromorphology shows tree roots, i.e. a fenced tree shrine; it was replaced by a pre-Aśokan brick-on-edge kerb and pavement (bricks 49 × 36 × 7 cm) and then enclosed by the Aśokan brick temple.
quote: yielded evidence of a sequence of human habitation between c.1300 BCE and sixth century CE … The first evidence of structural activity at the site of what was to become the Mayadevi Temple occurred in the middle of the sixth century BCE … the stratigraphy and soil sections suggest the presence of root systems, suggesting that a tree grew at this location
note: Agrees with the study and Mizutani (Rummindei, high). Adds the pre-Aśokan sequence (also summarised by Murakami 2016); a tree-centred shrine fits the tradition of the birth beside a tree that Xuanzang reports (his 無憂華樹, already withered), but nothing here dates the 7th-century state. No change to the rating. The volume is the 2nd edition (UNESCO 2019), not the 2013 edition named in literature.tsv.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Sacred Garden, Lumbini (Rummindei), Rupandehi, Nepal
evidence: Period VI, 'Gupta Lumbini' (3rd–9th c. CE): new square and stepped stūpas, the viharas V-1 and V-3 rebuilt, two Gupta temple basements S of the Mayadevi Temple, and a new carved-brick saptaratha temple holding the nativity image; Mishra reported 19 terracotta seals 'with Gupta characters' from a square Gupta stūpa (structure not specified). Bidari dates the 16 votive stūpas E of the temple (S-16) between the Chinese visits of the 7th c. and Ripu Malla's of 1312. The authors stress that the earlier excavators' datings are often unsupported.
quote: Period VI: Gupta Lumbini (third to ninth century CE) … Mishra also mentioned that 19 terracotta seals with Gupta characters were found at a square Gupta-period stupa … were constructed sometime between the visits of the Chinese travellers in the seventh century CE and Ripu Malla’s visit
note: Agrees: the site was being built on in the period of Xuanzang's visit, so his stūpas and temple belong to a living site. The 19 Gupta seals are unread here and might name the place; not followed up. No change to the rating.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Aśoka pillar, Lumbini (Rummindei), Rupandehi, Nepal
evidence: The pillar: polished Chunar sandstone, 37 t, originally 30 ft 10.5 in high of which 13 ft 8.5 in underground; set in a base slab on a brick foundation (Mishra); it tilts and has a vertical fissure down the middle; the top is broken, with no trace of the horse capital described by Xuanzang, but part of the base of the capital survives. The Oil River is not discussed.
quote: The pillar visibly tilts and has suffered some damage with a vertical fissure running down the middle. The top of the pillar is broken and there is no trace of the horse capital as described by Chinese traveller Xuanzang but part of the base of the capital survives.
note: Agrees (secure): the split shaft answers Xuanzang's pillar split down the middle by the nāga's thunderbolt; the surviving base of the capital is consistent with his lost horse capital. Adds measurements; nothing on the Tilar as Oil River.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Tilaurakot, Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: Ch. 8 (Coningham, Acharya, Manuel, Tremblay) on the UNESCO project from 2014: origins dated to 800 BCE by radiocarbon and OSL; occupation near the Samai Mai Temple from the 8th c. BCE; geophysics shows a street grid 'most likely' of the Kushan period (1st c. BCE–3rd c. CE), probably laid out centuries earlier; a palatial walled complex (the Central Walled Complex, CWC, with N, E, S and W gates), a brick water tank and monastic complexes; Gupta-style structures (carved brick, a large rectangular platform, dug 2018) under the modern Samai Mai Temple; the city was abandoned 'sometime in the first millennium CE'. They state Tilaurakot is 'widely identified' as Kapilavastu and that Mukherji found it by following Xuanzang. Nothing found names the place.
quote: Today’s Tilaurakot is widely identified as ancient Kapilavastu … After the city’s abandonment, sometime in the first millennium CE … confirm that the site’s origins date back to 800 BCE … This layout most likely dates to the Kushan period (first century BCE – third century CE) … have now been identified on a monumental structure under the modern Samai Mai Temple in Tilaurakot-Kapilavastu
note: Adds evidence on the Tilaurakot side of the open question (06.02): a planned walled town, with a palatial enclosure, and some Gupta-period building under Samai Mai, so the site was not wholly abandoned before Xuanzang's time; the abandonment date is not given. The identification is assumed, not argued; no inscription names Kapilavastu. Leaves the place open between Piprahwa–Ganwaria and Tilaurakot.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: stūpa and monastic complex outside the E side of Tilaurakot (Mukherji's Eastern Stupa)
evidence: Map key: 'Sites located outside the City … 18 The Eastern Stupa and Monastery', with Mukherji's 1899 plan of the stūpa; a hoard of 3rd-century-BCE silver punch-marked coins found at the monastic complex near the stūpa; walled ponds like those at Sisaniya lie around the Eastern Monastery. No identification with Xuanzang's monastery is made.
quote: 18 The Eastern Stupa and Monastery … Hoard of third century bce silver punch-marked coins discovered at the monastic complex near the stupa.
note: Bears on 06.02.x1 (Mukherji's building before the E gate): a monastic complex E of the city exists and has early material; nothing about its date in the 7th c. or a Sammitīya community. Inside the Tilaurakot frame only; stays open.

author: Coningham et al.
name_in_asr: Central Walled Complex (CWC); CWC - The Sangharama
asr_identification: the Central Walled Complex, centre of Tilaurakot
evidence: The geophysics and excavations revealed 'the remains of a palatial walled complex'; the site key lists the CWC with its northern, eastern, southern and western gates and 'CWC - The Sangharama', a monastery inside the palatial enclosure. No date or argument is given in this chapter.
quote: discovered, among others, the remains of a palatial walled complex, a brick water tank and monastic complexes … CWC - The Sangharama
note: Supports Murakami's observation (murakami2016:4) of a monastery-like building over the palace walls, which he compares with Xuanzang's vihāra on the site of Śuddhodana's hall. A parallel only, without a date or inscription; within the Tilaurakot frame; Ganwaria remains the alternative.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Niglihawa (Nigali Sagar) pillar, Kapilvastu district, Nepal; the town's location unknown
evidence: Two fragments of the pillar found in 1895, the upper half-submerged in the bank of the Niglisagar pond, the lower partly buried; the base and the plinth are missing, so its original location is unknown; the pillar was moved to its present spot in 1996. Faxian puts Kanakamuni's town about one yojana (c. 11–14 km) W of Kapilavastu, but Xuanzang's directions differ, so the town remains unlocated. The edict: Aśoka in his 14th year enlarged the Konakamana stūpa a second time, and came in his 20th year.
quote: inscriptions from Asoka and King Ripu Malla. It was moved to this … location in 1996 … As the base of the pillar and the plinth on which it once stood are missing, its original location remains unknown … However, Xuanzang provides different directions and, thus, the town’s location remains unknown.
note: Agrees with the study's caution (06.02.05a medium; whether the pillar is in situ is the question): the excavators find no base or plinth. Adds that the pillar was moved again in 1996, so its present spot is not the find-spot (the Niglisagar bank). Nothing decides between Araura-kot and Sisania Panre. Note: ch. 5 of the same volume (Stovel et al., p. 146) swaps the attributions ('Kanakamuni in Gotihawa and Krakuchanda in Niglihawa'), a slip.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Araurakot, Kapilvastu district, Nepal (a fortified enclosure)
evidence: Araurakot: an enclosure 270 × 270 m, clay ramparts brick-faced on S and E with stirrup bastions, a double moat on the W; mapped by Mukherji 1899; not excavated; geophysics 2015 found the interior largely empty except a raised SW platform with two buildings; its form resembles Kushan military outposts of the early 1st millennium CE; carved bricks like those of Lumbini, Kudan and Tilaurakot suggest occupation into the middle of the 1st millennium CE. No stūpa or Buddhist structure is reported.
quote: The site’s morphology bears a striking resemblance to the early first millennium ce military outposts found throughout the Kushan Empire … the interior was largely empty, except for a raised platform in the southwest corner with foundations of two buildings. Carved bricks similar to those from Lumbini, Kudan and Tilaurakot have been recovered from the site
note: Bears on Mukherji's Araura-kot for Kanakamuni's town (the in-situ branch of 06.02.05a): the site reads as a Kushan-type fort with an almost empty interior and no reported stūpa, which does not support a Buddha's natal town with a relic stūpa; it is not excavated, so not excluded. Kanakamuni's town stays near the pillar, unlocated.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Sagrahawa (Sagarwa), Kapilvastu district, N of Tilaurakot
evidence: Führer's excavations of 1896 exposed a large brick monument and smaller buildings on the W edge of the tank and 17 small brick stūpas to its SE, which he took for 'the place of the massacre' of the Śākyas that Xuanzang visited; from the centre of the large structure (twelve rooms of 2.7 × 3.0 m, similar to the cruciform temples at Kudan) a copper casket with bones, two gold nāga figures and semi-precious stones; geophysical surveys of 2016 and 2018 found further buried brick structures round the larger mound, 'a site of religious importance'.
quote: From the centre a copper casket … containing bones, two gold naga statues, … and semi-precious stones were recovered … Führer identified Sagrahawa as “the place of the massacre”, visited by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in the seventh century CE  … Geophysical surveys of subsurface archaeological features in 2016 and 2018 identified a series of additional buried brick structures
note: Reports Führer's identification (the study's only lead for 06.02.x9) without endorsing it; adds that the large structure resembles the 7th-century Kudan temples and that more buildings lie buried. No date or inscription; stays unlocated, Tilaurakot frame only.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Kudan, Kapilvastu district, S of Tilaurakot
evidence: Mukherji recorded four mounds (1899); Mitra (1962) exposed two large cruciform brick temples (Temple 1: 42.3 × 31.8 m, over 4.5 m high) on either side of a brick well dug to 3.7 m; from architecture and pottery she dated them to the 7th c. CE with 9th-c. elaborations; an octagonal Hindu temple c. 200 years old on another mound encases an older Śiva liṅga. 'Some scholars' take Kudan for the Nigrodhārāma, where the Buddha met his father and Rāhula was ordained.
quote: Mitra ascribed the construction of the temples to the seventh century CE , with later ninth century elaborations. Some scholars have suggested that Kudan may be the site of ancient Nigrodharama, the banyan grove where Gautama Buddha met his father
note: Reports Mukherji's line (Lori-Kudan) for 06.02.08 without deciding. The temples Mitra dug were Brahmanical (notes) and built around Xuanzang's time, which does not fit his Nyagrodha monastery; other mounds untested. Tilaurakot frame only; no change.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: tank at Kudan, Kapilvastu district (Vost 1906)
evidence: Site key for Kudan: the tank was probably dug for brick clay; 'Major Vost had suggested in 1906 that the tank was Hastigrata, where it is believed the elephant thrown by the Buddha landed'.
quote: The tank was probably created as … clay was extracted for making bricks. Major Vost had suggested in 1906 that the tank was Hastigrata, where it is believed the elephant thrown by the Buddha landed.
note: New to the study: Vost's (1906) Kudan tank for the elephant pit (象墮阬), against Mukherji's ditch 100 ft E of a mound S of Tilaurakot's S gate. The authors think the tank a borrow pit; a proposal by position in the Tilaurakot frame only. Stays unlocated.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Gotihawa, Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: A large brick stūpa, the stump of an Aśokan pillar and a water tank; Waddell dug the stūpa partly in 1898; Verardi's re-excavation (1990s; 2007 report): an initial stūpa 19.5 m across of concentric rings of rectangular and wedge-shaped, often incised, bricks, attributed to Aśoka, enlarged to 21.5 m with rectangular bricks in the Kushan period; occupation before the stūpa, radiocarbon 800 BCE, proto-NBPW. The surviving pillar piece is 3.2 m long and 79–83 cm thick; the inscribed part is broken off and lost. 'Some early archaeologists' took the site for Krakucchanda's birthplace.
quote: Some early archaeologists believed that the monuments marked the birthplace of Krakkuchanda Buddha, one of the earlier Buddhas … Verardi attributed the initial construction to Asoka (third century BCE) with an expansion during the Kushan period (100 BCE – 300 CE).
note: Agrees with the evidence the study already uses (Verardi via Falk): a Mauryan stūpa with a pillar stump beside it. Adds that the pillar's inscribed part is lost, so the pillar cannot name the Buddha. The authors do not commit to Krakucchanda. Study's Gotihawa (medium) unchanged.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Sisaniya (Sisania), Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: A mound 260 m long and a small circular mound 200 m N; Mukherji (1899) found a town with brick structures, mounds and a well; Mitra (1962) dated it to at least the 1st c. CE; Verardi's surface collection (1995) shows occupation up to the 9th c. CE; geophysics 2016 and 2018: a grid-plan settlement on a N–S road, a moat, a buried brick-lined tank, a walled pond between the town and the N mound, and an unexcavated stūpa 10 m across and 2 m high; possibly monastic complexes. No link to Xuanzang is made.
quote: Sisaniya comprises of a 260 metre long mound and a small circular mound 200 metres to its north … dated Sisaniya’s occupation up to the ninth century CE  … No archaeological investigation of the … stupa has been undertaken. It measures … ten metres in diameter and two metres in height.
note: Sisania is Mukherji's Arrow Well candidate in the Tilaurakot frame (06.02.10). Adds that it was occupied in Xuanzang's time and has a small stūpa and water features; nothing marks the spring. Remains the Tilaurakot-frame alternative to Birdpur; stays open.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: the Ramgram stūpa near Parasi, Nawalparasi, Nepal
evidence: The stūpa is 10 m high and 23.5 m across, on an island formed by an old oxbow of the Jharahi River and a modern canal; Rijal identified it as Rāmagrāma from Faxian's and Xuanzang's itineraries; geophysical surveys in 1997, 1999 and 2018 found several quadrangular brick monasteries (one a 'perfect quadrangular Kushan monastery' under the 'unlucky field') and a water tank W and N of the stūpa; S. S. Shrestha's excavations (1999–2004) date the site's establishment between the Mauryan and Gupta periods.
quote: Referencing the itineraries of the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang, B.K. Rijial of Nepal’s Department of Archaeology identified the stupa as Ramagrama … These identified the presence of several quadrangular brick monasteries and a water tank to the west and north of the stupa.
note: Agrees with the study's best candidate for 06.03 (Parāsi stūpa, low). Adds the geophysical results the note lists as not yet in hand: monasteries and a water tank beside the stūpa; Xuanzang has a monastery near the stūpa and a nāga pond. Nothing names the place; the water tank may bear on the pond. Rating could be reviewed but no inscription.

author: Coningham et al.
asr_identification: Bhandarkhal, Pashupati, Kathmandu valley, Nepal
evidence: Geophysics, auger cores and three trenches (2014–16) at Bhandarkhal: an earthen-edged monumental tank (attributed to the early Licchavi period by Pracchia/Di Castro), a robbed brick platform with stone drain, roof tiles, a Pashupati coin, a stamped sherd with 4½ Licchavi characters; scientific dates still awaited. Licchavi inscriptions of the 5th c. CE show the hillside was densely occupied. Xuanzang and the capital are not discussed.
quote: interpreted as a monumental tank and attributed to the early Licchavi period on the basis of artefactual evidence … We also uncovered a Pashupati coin with a depiction of the Yogi
note: Not relevant to the location: Licchavi-period remains at Deopatan/Pashupati, consistent with the Kathmandu valley (07.05), which no one doubts; nothing about the capital Xuanzang reports or its site. literature.tsv's 07.05 is correct but the item adds nothing to code.

author: Murakami
name_in_asr: カピラ城; ティラウラコット（Tilaurakot）
asr_identification: Tilaurakot, Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: Summary of the UNESCO/JFIT Phase 2 work (2014–17, Durham and DoA): recut of Mitra's N rampart (2013) found 9 post holes under the brick rampart, dating the fortification to about the 6th c. BCE; about 20 post holes N of Samai Mai give settlement from the 8th c. BCE; a central tank 30 × 30 m, first used in the Mauryan period; a planned fortified city 450 m E–W × 500 m N–S, 23 km W of Lumbini. He reviews Mishra (700 BCE–200 CE), Rijal (PGW, NBP; 8th–7th c. BCE), Rissho University 1967–77 (4th c. BCE–mid-3rd c. CE) and UNESCO 1999 (Mound V). Concludes the probability that Tilaurakot is Kapilavastu is higher. He states Piprahwa–Ganwaria are monastic sites and so out of the search if Kapilavastu means the royal city, which 'many scholars' accept.
quote: サマ イ・マイや北側城壁の調査によって，ティラウラコットにおける人間の定住時期 を紀元前 8 世紀，城塞化を紀元前 6 世紀と推定し，Debala Mitra の学説を改めて 否定している … ティラウラコットのカピラ城である 蓋然性はさらに高まっているというべきであろう
note: Adds to the Tilaurakot side of 06.02 (open), but the dates are those of Davis, Coningham et al. 2016 already in the note; nothing names Kapilavastu. The author's sect (法華宗陣門流) funds the Durham excavation (p. 237). He makes Mitra (1972) place Kapilavastu at Ganwaria; the study has that from Srivastava. Does not resolve the question; place stays open.

author: Murakami
name_in_asr: 城外東側に位置する仏塔（Mound XI）; 巨大な僧院複合施設 (Monastic Complex)
asr_identification: monastic complex S of the stūpa Mound XI, outside the E side of Tilaurakot
evidence: Geophysics round the stūpa Mound XI outside the E side of the city revealed a huge monastic complex 250 m N–S × 100 m E–W adjoining the stūpa on the S; at the S end of the monastery's boundary wall a terracotta pot with 497 punch-marked coins. He compares Xuanzang's monastery beside the palace city with 3,000 Sammitīya monks (T51:900c) and says the complex 'recalls' it.
quote: 仏塔の南に隣接するエリアに南北 250 m × 東西 100 m の巨大な僧 院複合施設 （Monastic Complex）の存在が明らかになった … 僧院境界壁の南端からはテラコッタの壺 に入った 497 枚のパンチマークコイン（打刻印銀貨）が発見され … 城外東側で確認された 巨大僧院は玄奘の記述を彷彿とさせ
note: Adds a candidate in the Tilaurakot frame that agrees in position with Mukherji's building before the E gate (06.02.x1): a large monastery E of the city. No date for its 7th-century use (the coin hoard is 3rd c. BCE, Coningham et al. 2019), no inscription; tentative. Depends on Tilaurakot (06.02 open).

author: Murakami
name_in_asr: カンタカ・ストゥーパ (Mound XI)
asr_identification: stūpa Mound XI outside the E side of Tilaurakot
evidence: By local tradition the stūpa Mound XI E of the city is called the Kanthaka stūpa and associated with the prince's departure; Murakami says this needs verification.
quote: 伝承によれば，この仏塔は カンタカ・ストゥーパとも呼ばれ，釈尊の出家と関連付けされる向きもあるが， その正否は今後の検証を要する
note: A traditional name only, untested by the author; bears on the vihāra where the prince left the city (06.02.x7), unlocated (Mukherji: near the gate before 06.02.x1, or Sandwā). Tilaurakot frame only; stays unlocated.

author: Murakami
name_in_asr: 四方を壁で囲われた巨大建造物 (Central Walled Complex), Mound V; 建造物 A
asr_identification: Central Walled Complex at Mound V, Tilaurakot; building A on its N side
evidence: Geophysics in 2015 at Mound V showed a walled complex 100 × 100 m with a 1.5 m brick wall; excavation from January 2016 (70 × 20 m on the N side) found a strong N gate and, E of it, building A with ten or more rooms (c. 5.0 × 3.5 m, walls 40 cm) built on top of the brick wall of the complex. He takes the complex for the palace of Faxian's 白浄王の故宮 and Xuanzang's 浄飯王の正殿, and compares building A with Xuanzang's vihāra built over the hall, without asserting the match; other buildings over the complex appear in the geophysics.
quote: 建造物は東西 100 m × 南北 100 m の大きさで，周囲を 1.5 m 幅の煉瓦壁で囲われ ている … 宮殿の煉瓦壁の上にこの建造物 A が建てられていることであり … 現時点で建造物 A が玄奘の記録と照合し 得るものとは断定できないが，極めて興味深い事象であると考えられる
note: Adds site evidence to the Tilaurakot alternative for 06.02.x2 (Mukherji placed the hall in the NW area): a walled enclosure in the centre with a monastic building over its wall, the arrangement Xuanzang describes (精舍 over the hall). Undated, no inscription; the palace reading is an inference. Ganwaria (Srivastava) remains the alternative; the parent is open.

author: Murakami
asr_identification: Mayadevi Temple, Lumbini (Rummindei), Nepal
evidence: Summary of Phase 1 (2010–13): 21 trenches at the Mayadevi Temple, garden, village mound, well and helipad; a pre-Aśokan timber shrine round a sacred tree; radiocarbon from room C5 of the temple puts the shrine in the mid-6th c. BCE; the village mound settled about 1300 BCE. Mentions the JBF excavation of 1992–95 and its marker stone.
quote: 最初期のマヤ堂は聖樹を祀り，その周囲を木材のフェンスで囲った祠堂 （Timber shrine）であったと考えられること … ルンビニにおける人 間の定住時期が村の塚（Village Mound）の調査により，紀元前 1300 年頃と推定さ れた
note: Agrees (Rummindei, high); secondary summary of Coningham et al. 2013 (Antiquity), same evidence as coningham2013_sacred_garden:1.

author: Strickland et al.
asr_identification: Lohasariya, low mound c. 150 m S of Tilaurakot
evidence: The low mound c. 150 m S of the city (50 × 30 m), thick with slag, which Mukherji's 1899 plan marked as one of Kapilavastu's cardinal stūpas (Allen 2008) and his 1901 report as an iron workshop. Trench S (4 × 3 m, 2012) beside Rijal's 1970s sondage: an artificially raised mound with slag and furnace lining; radiocarbon early 6th–late 5th c. BCE (lowest), 373–199 BCE (mound raising), 198–105 BCE (furnace entrance); nearly 8 t of slag, iron smelting or smithing; geophysics 2014 (2.7 ha) shows possible furnaces and a possible second moat S of the known moat. No stūpa or Buddhist remain is reported.
quote: Tilaurakot’s southern industrial mound, known locally as Lohasariya, is a low mound located approximately 150 metres south of the ancient city … Mukherj initially identified the mound as one of ancient Kapilavastu’s cardinal stupas (Allen 2008: 191) … we may confirm that the southern mound hosted a major industrial complex from the fourth century BCE onwards.
note: Bears on the stūpas S of the city in the Tilaurakot frame: the mound c. 150 m (about 500 ft) S is probably Mukherji's 'small mound c. 500 ft S of the S gate' (06.02.x4) and lies near his Derwa mounds a furlong S (06.02.x11); the identity is inferred from the distances, not stated. It is an iron-working mound, not a stūpa, so it does not support either stūpa there. Both stay unlocated.

author: Mori (UNESCO/University of Tokyo)
asr_identification: 99 sites in Rupandehi district (Lumbini itself excluded)
evidence: Draft site catalogue (ver. 2, May 2017; survey April 2016 and February–March 2017) by T. Mori, University of Tokyo: one form per site with coordinates, remains and condition; 235 sites mapped (136 Kapilbastu, 99 Rupandehi), 'except for Lumbini'. Several mounds near Lumbini are described as stūpa-shaped (e.g. Sagara Manauri, 27.4726, 83.2460), without excavation, date or identification; no site is linked to Xuanzang or Faxian. Niglihawa (Kapilbastu district) is not among the Rupandehi forms.
quote: The map shows 235 archeological sites, 136 sites in Kapilbastu and 99 sites in Rupandehi, except for Lumbini.
note: No bearing on 06.02.11 or 06.02.05a: Lumbini is excluded and Nigali Sagar lies outside the district. A reference list for later route work E of Lumbini (towards 06.03) only. The text is the 2017 draft, not the 2019 edition named in literature.tsv.
